precepts.text: This is Jacob talking: twenty years have I been with thee; that which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it. In the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night. I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times. Laban was a grimy dude, man. He did Jacob dirty: yo, man, you changed my wages, my paycheck is all low, I'm taking care of your cattle, you're doing me wrong over here.
precepts.point: So Jacob was Laban's shepherd. He took care of the sheep, the cattle. He was a shepherd just like Abel was a shepherd, and Esau was the man of the field just like Cain was a man of the field. You see where I'm going with this?

note.label: As in the Days of Noah: Past & Present

precepts.why:
Rebekah told Jacob to flee to her brother Laban's house because Esau wanted him dead, so he ran to Laban, and “Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks.” He took rods of green poplar, hazel and chesnut, “pilled white strakes in them,” and set them before the flocks at the watering troughs. The stronger cattle conceived among the rods, “so the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s.” “And the man increased exceedingly.”

So Jacob was Laban's shepherd; he took care of the sheep and the cattle. He was a shepherd just as Abel was a shepherd, and Esau was the man of the field just as Cain was a man of the field. The same two lines keep repeating.

And Jacob tells what that shepherding cost him: “This twenty years have I been with thee;” “That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it.” “Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.” “I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattle: and thou hast changed my wages ten times.”

Laban was a grimy man. He did Jacob dirty: Jacob took care of his cattle day and night, bore the losses himself, and Laban kept lowering his pay. Yet God increased Jacob exceedingly in spite of it.

precepts.text: Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain; Rachel's beauty did not keep her from being a thief.
precepts.point: Laban went to shear his sheep, and Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's. Remember what we read in Proverbs about beauty: yes, she was fine, but she was a thief. She might have been a fine thief, but she was a thief.

note.label: Genesis 31: The Return Home and Laban's Idols

precepts.why:
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.”

Remember that as Jacob rises up to return home to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan, and “Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s.” Yes, she was fine, but she was a thief. She might have been a fine thief, but she was a thief. Her beauty did not keep her from stealing, and it is not beauty that earns praise but the fear of the Lord.

precepts.text: Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah the father of Abraham and the father of Nachor, and they served other gods; Laban came of that idolatrous house.
precepts.point: Jacob answered that he went away because he was afraid Laban would take his daughters from him by force, and said, With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live. For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them.

note.label: Genesis 31: The Return Home and Laban's Idols

precepts.why:
“Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods.” Terah and his house served other gods, and Laban was of the house of Nahor.

That is why Laban's question tells you what he was: “wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?” Laban was an idolater, just like his fathers on the other side of the flood. Jacob answered that he went away because he was afraid Laban would take his daughters from him by force, and, not knowing that Rachel had stolen them, said, “With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live”.

precepts.text: The Most High told Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred; he separated Abram from the idolaters.
precepts.point: Jacob answered that he went away because he was afraid Laban would take his daughters from him by force, and said, With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live. For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them.

note.label: Genesis 31: The Return Home and Laban's Idols

precepts.why:
“Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee”.

Here is why the Most High separated Abram from his country and his kindred: they served other gods. Laban, of the house of Nahor, asking Jacob “wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?” shows what that kindred was, idolaters. The Most High separated Abram because of what He had set up for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and for us, that we not be idolaters.

precepts.text: Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's; that is where the strange gods in the household came from.
precepts.point: From Eve to Rachel the scriptures warn how sin enters through the household; of the woman came the beginning of sin. Sisters, stay in the spirit and guard against the serpent's beguiling as the mothers were beguiled.

note.label: Genesis 35: Bethel and the Twelve Sons of Israel

precepts.why:
“And Laban went to shear his sheep: and Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s.” That is where the strange gods in Jacob's household came from.

When God sent Jacob up to Bethel, Jacob told his household, “Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean”. The images Rachel stole from Laban were those strange gods: idolatry hidden in the household that had to be put away before he could stand at Bethel. Rachel finally gave them up, and Jacob hid them under the oak by Shechem.

precepts.text: Rachel hid the images in the camel's furniture and sat upon them, and Laban found them not.
precepts.point: From Eve to Rachel the scriptures warn how sin enters through the household; of the woman came the beginning of sin. Sisters, stay in the spirit and guard against the serpent's beguiling as the mothers were beguiled.

note.label: Genesis 35: Bethel and the Twelve Sons of Israel

precepts.why:
“Now Rachel had taken the images, and put them in the camel’s furniture, and sat upon them. And Laban searched all the tent, but found them not.” She told her father she could not rise, “for the custom of women is upon me”, and “he searched, but found not the images.”

So the idols stayed hidden in the household until Jacob said, “Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean”. Idolatry hidden in the household must be put away before you can stand at Bethel. What Rachel sat on and hid from Laban, she finally gave up, and Jacob hid the images under the oak by Shechem.

moments.label: SHE REVERENCE HER HUSBAND: Submission, Grace & Self-Examination of a Biblical Wife

points: And she said to her father, Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before thee; for the custom of women is upon me. She is saying, I have my period, so that is why I am not getting up. They did not have maxi pads with wings. She said, if I get up it is going to run all down, it is going to stink up in here, I am going to offend you.

Now merely it was an evil that she did that, because she was sitting on idolatrous items. But the point was the rising itself. Husbands, if you get that greeting and it is sincere, then great. How often does your wife greet you when you come home, at the door? It does not happen. Kids will do it a lot more, and the pets will for sure — well, not cats. Even if they do come up to you they will not even touch you, they just walk up like, oh, you here now?

note.label: SHE REVERENCE HER HUSBAND: Submission, Grace & Self-Examination of a Biblical Wife

points: Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons, saying, Jacob hath taken away all that was our father's, and of that which was our father's hath he gotten all this glory; and Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and behold, it was not toward him as before.

Remember, Laban had just acknowledged, I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake; now he is looking at Jacob sideways because of what his sons said. That is exactly why Jacob said, So shall my righteousness answer for me: he dealt righteously in the open so his dealings would be his answer.

note.label: Genesis 31: The Return Home and Laban's Idols
